# Mode {#sec-mode}

{{< include ../preamble.qmd >}}

::: {style="margin-top: 1em; font-size: 125%; font-weight: 1000; text-align: center;"}
Chameau unimodal, dromadaire bimodal
:::

In French, *la mode* (feminine) means fashion, while *le mode* (masculine) refers to the statistical mode. Yet, fashion is precisely the concept behind the statistical mode^[A british statistican defined the term, then french academics integrated the concept and decided that it should be masculine to fit their principles].  Conceptually, the statistical mode simply represents the most popular category, closely reflecting its everyday meaning. Looking at a distribution (@sec-distribution), its interpretation is straightforward: it is the value or category with the highest frequency.

The mode is one of three main metrics used to measure central tendency, along with the mean (@sec-mean) and the median (@sec-median). Unlike the mean and median, the mode works for qualitative and quantitative variables, and it is especially useful for the former. While most people are accustomed to calculating the mean, computing the mode is less common in daily life. Nevertheless, it is easy to identify from a distribution (@sec-distribution).

## Formal {.unnumbered}

The mode is the value that appears most often in a dataset. If $X$ is a qualitative or discrete variable, the mode is the value $x$ with the highest frequency of occurrence. For a continuous variable, the mode corresponds to the bin with the highest frequency, which means the exact mode depends on the choice of bin size and boundaries.

A mode does not have to be unique. Distributions can have multiple local peak values, leading to bimodal or multimodal distributions.

Finally, in the rare case where a distribution is completely flat—meaning all values occur with the exact same frequency—the mode does not exist.

## Examples {.unnumbered}

The mode is generally inferred directly from a visual distribution.

- For categorical/qualitative variables:
Mouse is the single mode (unimodal) on the left, whereas both catta and mouse are modes (bimodal) on the right.
```{r}
df_lemur <- data.frame(
    species = c("indri", "catta", "mouse"),
    value = c(10, 20, 300),
    valueb = c(10, 30, 30)
)

# Colors
col_base <- "#94a3b8"
col_mode <- "#e11d48"

# Set layout for two side-by-side plots
par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))

# Plot A: Unimodal
cols_a <- c(col_base, col_base, col_mode)
b_a <- barplot(
  height = df_lemur$value,
  names.arg = rep("", 3),
  ylab = "Count",
  col = cols_a,
  border = NA,
  las = 1,
  ylim = c(0, 320)
)
grid(nx = NA, ny = NULL, col = "#e2e8f0", lty = 1)
barplot(height = df_lemur$value, col = cols_a, border = NA, add = TRUE, las = 1)
axis(1, at = b_a[1:2], labels = df_lemur$species[1:2], tick = FALSE, col.axis = "#475569")
axis(1, at = b_a[3], labels = df_lemur$species[3], tick = FALSE, col.axis = col_mode, font = 2)

# Plot B: Bimodal
cols_b <- c(col_base, col_mode, col_mode)
b_b <- barplot(
  height = df_lemur$valueb,
  names.arg = rep("", 3),
  ylab = "Count",
  col = cols_b,
  border = NA,
  las = 1,
  ylim = c(0, 35)
)
grid(nx = NA, ny = NULL, col = "#e2e8f0", lty = 1)
barplot(height = df_lemur$valueb, col = cols_b, border = NA, add = TRUE, las = 1)
axis(1, at = b_b[1], labels = df_lemur$species[1], tick = FALSE, col.axis = "#475569")
axis(1, at = b_b[2:3], labels = df_lemur$species[2:3], tick = FALSE, col.axis = col_mode, font = 2)

# Reset plotting layout
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```


- For discrete variables:
The mode is 4, as it has the highest count.

```{r}
set.seed(1)
df_discrete <- data.frame(size = rpois(100, 5))
df_discrete <- aggregate(n ~ size, data = transform(df_discrete, n = 1), FUN = length)

# Find mode
mode_val <- df_discrete$size[which.max(df_discrete$n)]
col_vector <- ifelse(df_discrete$size == mode_val, "#e11d48", "#64748b")

par(mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))
plot(
  df_discrete$size, df_discrete$n,
  type = "n",
  xlab = "Size",
  ylab = "Count",
  xaxt = "n",
  las = 1,
  bty = "l"
)
grid(nx = NA, ny = NULL, col = "#e2e8f0", lty = 1)

# Draw stem lines and points
segments(
  x0 = df_discrete$size, y0 = 0,
  x1 = df_discrete$size, y1 = df_discrete$n,
  col = col_vector, lwd = 2
)
points(df_discrete$size, df_discrete$n, pch = 16, cex = 1.4, col = col_vector)

# Highlighted axis labels
non_modes <- df_discrete$size[df_discrete$size != mode_val]
axis(1, at = non_modes, labels = non_modes, col.axis = "#475569")
axis(1, at = mode_val, labels = mode_val, col.axis = "#e11d48", font = 2)
```


- More care is needed when identifying the mode of a continuous variable from a histogram. Because bin widths and boundaries are arbitrary, different binning choices can alter which bin appears as the mode.


```{r}
set.seed(123)
df_quant <- data.frame(size = rnorm(100, 10, 1))

par(mfrow = c(1, 2), mar = c(4, 4, 2, 1))

plot_hist_with_mode <- function(data, bin_width) {
  brks <- seq(floor(min(data$size)), ceiling(max(data$size)), by = bin_width)
  h <- hist(data$size, breaks = brks, plot = FALSE)

  max_idx <- which.max(h$counts)
  cols <- rep("#94a3b8", length(h$counts))
  cols[max_idx] <- "#e11d48"

  plot(h, col = cols, border = "white", main = "", xlab = "Size", ylab = "Frequency", las = 1, xaxt = "n")
  grid(nx = NA, ny = NULL, col = "#e2e8f0", lty = 1)
  plot(h, col = cols, border = "white", add = TRUE, las = 1)

  # Standard tick marks and labels
  axis(1, col.axis = "#475569")

  # Mode midpoint value
  mode_mid <- h$mids[max_idx]

  # Y-position for the text (placed slightly higher than standard tick labels, without any tick mark)
  y_pos <- par("usr")[3] - (diff(par("usr")[3:4]) * 0.035)

  text(
    x = mode_mid,
    y = y_pos,
    labels = round(mode_mid, 1),
    col = "#e11d48",
    font = 2,
    xpd = TRUE,
    adj = c(0.5, 0)
  )
}

# Plot A: Binwidth = 1
plot_hist_with_mode(df_quant, 1)

# Plot B: Binwidth = 0.2
plot_hist_with_mode(df_quant, 0.2)

# Reset layout
par(mfrow = c(1, 1))
```


## Tips and warnings {.unnumbered}

- The mode equals the mean and median only when the distribution is symmetric and unimodal, such as in a standard bell-shaped curve.
- There is a common rule of thumb stating that for a right-skewed distribution, mode > median > mean (and the reverse for a left-skewed distribution). While useful to know theoretically, this relationship has little practical application.
- Always inspect the distribution before running statistical tests, as most standard tests are not designed for multimodal data. If a distribution is bimodal or multimodal, special analytical steps must be taken.
